# Osprey/FID-A Edited MRS Processing Notes
These notes are a compact offline oracle for the task. They summarize public
Osprey/FID-A workflow concepts and standard edited magnetic resonance

## Osprey and FID-A
Osprey is an all-in-one software suite for processing and quantitative analysis
of in-vivo magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) data. Its workflow separates
loading, preprocessing, fitting, quantification, and reporting. FID-A is an
open-source MATLAB toolbox used for MRS simulation and processing. Osprey
bundles and builds on FID-A-style data structures and processing functions.
An MRS dataset is often represented in two linked forms:
- `fids`: complex time-domain free induction decay samples;
- `specs`: frequency-domain spectra obtained by Fourier transform.
The structure also carries axes and dimension metadata such as time, averages,
and subspectra. Operations that scale or phase a spectrum generally need to keep
the time-domain and frequency-domain representations consistent.
## Edited MRS Subspectra
Edited MRS methods such as MEGA editing, HERMES, and HERCULES acquire multiple
related subspectra. Each subspectrum corresponds to a different editing
condition. The final analysis often combines or subtracts these conditions so
that an edited metabolite signal can be isolated from stronger overlapping
background resonances.
This means the subspectra are not independent unrelated experiments. They are
paired or grouped observations of the same sample under different acquisition
conditions. Common resonances should remain comparable across subspectra before
alignment and combination.
## Phase and Polarity
A 180 degree phase shift changes the sign of a real-valued resonance peak. In a
simple picture, a positive peak at a reference resonance becomes a negative peak

45	For edited MRS processing, this is not a cosmetic plotting issue. Frequency and
46	phase alignment procedures assume that common reference features have compatible
47	polarity. Difference spectra also assume that the signals being subtracted have
48	the intended sign relationship. If a common reference peak is accidentally
49	opposite signed before alignment, the algorithm can estimate the wrong
50	correction or produce a difference spectrum with suppressed signal.
51	
52	Stable singlet-like resonances, commonly including creatine-like signal around
53	3 ppm in proton MRS examples, are frequently used as reference features for
54	quality checks, frequency/phase correction, or polarity assessment.
55	
56	## Load Stage and Process Stage
57	
58	An MRS processing pipeline can manipulate phase or polarity at more than one
59	stage. A loader may split raw acquisition rows into subspectra and may also undo
60	phase cycling. A later processing stage may classify subspectra, estimate
61	polarity, align them, and combine or subtract them.
62	
63	These stages are coupled. If the loader removes or changes polarity information
64	too early, the processing stage may no longer be able to determine how the
65	subspectra should be aligned. Conversely, if the process stage assumes all
66	subspectra are already polarity-consistent when they are not, alignment and
67	combination can be scientifically invalid.

```matlab
function [x, fval] = sb_lm(fun, x0, lb, ub)
% damped Gauss-Newton least squares on residual vector fun(x)
x = x0(:);
r = fun(x);  f = sum(r(:).^2)/2;
for it = 1:60
    J = sb_fdjac(fun, x, r);
    g = J.'*r;
    A = J.'*J;
    mu = 1e-6*max(diag(A)+eps);
    solved = false;
    for inner = 1:12
        step = -(A + mu*eye(size(A))) \ g;
        xn = x + step;
        if ~isempty(lb), xn = max(xn, lb(:)); end
        if ~isempty(ub), xn = min(xn, ub(:)); end
        rn = fun(xn); fn = sum(rn(:).^2)/2;
        if isfinite(fn) && fn < f
            x = xn; r = rn; f = fn; solved = true;
            mu = max(mu/10, eps);
            break;
        end
        mu = mu*10;
    end
    if ~solved || norm(step) < 1e-10*(1+norm(x)), break; end
end
fval = f;
end
```
